posts.text: NEW BIS RULE – The BIS rule tightens US AI-chip export controls to stop Chinese companies bypassing restrictions by renting computing power from overseas data centres rather than buying chips directly. Released yesterday by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, it was written by and at the direction of Treasury and the National Security Council. It formally rescinds the earlier, unenforced AI Diffusion Rule.It introduces licensing requirements for advanced chips and servers used by data centres worldwide to provide substantial computing capacity to Chinese and other restricted companies. It also adds chip-export licensing requirements for Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, and tightens customer checks and foundry controls, with certain exemptions for US-headquartered recipients and commercial recommendation systems. The aim is to close the offshore-compute loophole and protect US national security. The likely impact is higher compliance costs and greater uncertainty for chip suppliers and cloud operators, potentially more expensive or restricted access to advanced compute for Chinese AI developers, and delays to affected chip shipments and data-centre projects—not a blanket ban on overseas AI investment. Tighter compute access is also seen as a risk to AI model training and Chinese cloud revenue growth. Licence approvals will be considered case by case.

Those same 4 stacks power EVs, humanoids, and industrial robotics.

Risks are real: certification, safety, cost per kWh, range at 400km / 300kmh is still short-haul only.

Congratulations to Alvin Lim, CFA, CMT and Climate Bridge International on a genuine first: Singapore’s first Article 6 Letter of Authorisation, issued by Rwanda.

A couple of reasons this resonates with me.

Rwanda. I’ve seen firsthand atAkagera National Park - Rwanda andNyungwe National Park-Rwanda what happens when the Rwandan government pairs clear rules with long-term partnerships. Capital follows, and results follow capital. This authorisation applies the same discipline to carbon.

Predictability. Globally, more than 348 million credits have been authorised for transfer under Article 6.2, yet only around 150,000 have been delivered. Authorisation is the start line, not the finish. What closes that gap is exactly what this post describes: predictable approvals and risk-sharing that let developers commit capital years before the first credit is issued.

Indonesia is moving in the same direction. Approval timelines are now written into regulation, and our first Article 6 purchase agreement was signed with Norway last week.

The next test is delivery. I look forward to seeing the first issuance.

What does it take to make nature investable?

Our #WALDInnovationFacility discussion at#COP31 brought together government, development finance, project developers, carbon-market standards and investors to tackle that question from different angles.

Four messages stood out:
1. Investment readiness has to be built. Project design, safeguards, carbon and biodiversity evidence, community participation, governance and sound economics all need investment before larger pools of capital can engage.
2. Integrity and investability should reinforce each other. Investing in quality early can reduce downstream risk and strengthen investor confidence.
3. Catalytic finance has a distinct role. Public and concessional resources can finance the difficult preparation stage that markets often cannot.
4. Carbon finance will not always be enough on its own. Some projects will need complementary or blended sources of capital to deliver high-integrity climate, biodiversity and community outcomes at scale.

Many thanks toSandeep Sengupta (IUCN), Friederike Kärcher Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), Jeff Silverman (Conservation International), Liz Guinessey (Verra), Tracy Lane (KPMG Kenya), Joseph Hutabarat (Fauna & Flora Indonesia) and Nicolai Tust (KfW) and participants for a candid, practical conversation, and to Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) andKfW for the partnership withIUCN behind the Facility.

ForWALD Phase II, the direction is clear: build the pipeline, finance integrity early, and generate the evidence needed to move credible nature-based projects from promising concepts towards implementation, investment and scale.

"Enhancing Formation Test Interpretation Using Borehole Image Logs in Heterogeneous Reservoirs, South Sumatra Basin."

What will we share?
Formation testing in heterogeneous reservoirs can be challenging due to lithological variations, fracture-controlled fluid pathways, and limited matrix permeability. These conditions can lead to misleading interpretations, including tight formations, lost seal tests, and unexpected water production.

This study highlights the importance of an integrated subsurface approach in improving formation evaluation and reducing interpretation uncertainties in exploration wells.

I'm excited to share; I'm looking for two people to join me at Nafas Foundation! Indonesia's air quality science and technology non-profit organisation.

Over the past few years, air quality in Indonesia increasingly become national conversation. Unfortunately, it has once again become Southeast Asia's primary concerns this year.

When I first started air quality, I was fascinated by the science itself (as an atmospheric science nerd). Over time, curiosity evolved into something crucial: understanding how science and technology interact with society. 

📖  The very reason, I chose to study Science in Society. What began as an enthusiasm for generating new form of knowledge, was evolved into a different set of social-discipline questions:

What happens after the evidence exists? 
What happens after the data is produced? 
How do people make sense of it? 
How do institutions respond to it? 
And what helps turn knowledge into action?

These questions led me to moments of reflection on what works best in Indonesia.

While air pollution may be a shared challenge, the air we experience is deeply local, especially in Indonesia, where evidence is effective when it is grounded in local realities and connected to local needs, capacities, and priorities.

In a country as diverse as Indonesia, with its rich cultures, histories, languages, and lived realities, every place has its own context, ecosystem, priorities, capacities, and challenges. Solutions work in one place less likely 'simply' be transplanted to another. The understanding of local realities with the people who know the realities, works best for a lasting progress.

At Nafas Foundation, we're investing in a locally led approach to air quality, strengthening community-based outdoor monitoring networks (continuing five years of local volunteers) and working alongside communities, researchers, governments, and partners to build a better understanding of local air quality from the ground up. Increasingly, we're seeing local knowledge serve as a compass for a collaborative decision-making at local government level!

Two new data centres opened in Jakarta this month. Each one needs a team that can run it every hour of the year.

On 1 November, LG CNS completed a 30 MW AI data centre in Jakarta for KMG, a joint venture of Sinar Mas Group and Korea Investment Real Asset Management. LG CNS says customers took the full capacity before construction finished. Later phases could take incoming power to 400 MW.

The buildings get the headlines. The people who keep them running get less attention. A site that promises uptime all year needs a site head, engineers who know power and cooling, and someone who can manage clients on strict contracts.

Every new operator will look first at the people who have already run a facility like this. That group is small, so it helps to look further.

Two suggestions for companies building or expanding in this sector.

Look at adjacent industries. Power plants, large manufacturing sites and telecom networks also run critical equipment around the clock, and their leaders know what an outage costs.

Hire the site leader before commissioning. That person should help choose the team that will run the site, not inherit one.

10th Biogas Biomass Bioenergy Asia Summit 2026 – Indonesia Focus, part of the ASEAN Energy Transition & Decarbonization Summit 2026.
For Participation & Cooperation Inquiry: If you are interested in attending, sponsoring, partnering or learning more about the summit, please feel free to contact our team via email: dl@inbcglobal.com.
The Summit will be held on November 26th–27th, 2026 at Hotel Bidakara Jakarta, Indonesia, bringing together 350+ industry leaders, project owners, technology providers, investors, EPC companies and policymakers across the regional bioenergy value chain.
For companies involved in Biogas, Biomethane, Bio-CNG, POME treatment, Anaerobic Digestion, Biogas Upgrading, CHP or Waste-to-Energy, we believe Indonesia is becoming an increasingly important market for project development and technology deployment.
Why Indonesia’s Biogas Market Is Worth Watching
Indonesia has a large base of palm oil mills and agro-industrial facilities, creating significant opportunities for converting POME and other organic waste streams into renewable energy and higher-value products.

Who Will You Meet?
The Summit is designed to connect companies across the complete biogas project value chain, including:
Palm Oil Mills & POME Project Owners | Biogas & Biomethane Developers | IPPs & Renewable Energy Developers |
EPC Contractors | Biogas Upgrading & Gas Treatment Technology Providers | CHP & Gas Engine Suppliers |
Wastewater & Anaerobic Digestion Companies | Investors & Financiers | Energy & Utility Companies | Government & Policymakers

This makes the event particularly relevant if your company is looking to:
→ Identify new Indonesian biogas / biomethane projects
→ Meet POME and industrial wastewater project owners
→ Develop partnerships with local EPCs and developers
→ Introduce biogas upgrading, Bio-CNG or CHP technologies
→ Explore biomethane and green gas opportunities
→ Identify investment or project development opportunities
→ Build business relationships in Indonesia and the wider ASEAN market
